analysis.one_liner: Taxes large federal contractors to fund public financing of Senate elections.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2011, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies holding more than $10 million in federal contracts would pay a 0.5% excise tax on the money the government pays them, capped at $500,000 per company per year. The revenue would be designated for a "Fair Elections Fund" to publicly finance Senate elections. Companies receiving the most federal money — defense contractors, IT firms, and other major suppliers — would bear the cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain the most: Senate candidates would be able to run campaigns on public money instead of relying on large donors, including the very contractors the tax applies to, which weakens the connection between federal contracts and campaign fundraising. Small-dollar donors and citizens without wealth to contribute also gain a more level playing field. The companies that would pay the tax are large government contractors, not individuals.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a dedicated revenue stream for a Fair Elections Fund to publicly finance Senate elections, reducing candidates' dependence on large private donations and on contractors who win federal work.
By charging the tax to the companies receiving contract payments, it shifts some campaign financing burden away from ordinary taxpayers and small donors.

analysis.who_pays: Companies with more than $10 million in annual federal contracts — defense contractors, IT and services firms, and other major suppliers to the government — would pay 0.5% of contract payments, up to $500,000 per year. Any added cost could be passed on through contract prices, in which case taxpayers would bear part of it indirectly.

drawbacks.text: The tax is a new cost on government contractors, which some would argue gets passed through to the prices agencies pay, meaning taxpayers could partly foot the bill for the fund themselves.

The link between the tax and the Fair Elections Fund is only a nonbinding 'sense of the Senate' — the bill does not actually require the revenue to be appropriated for public financing, so the money could legally be spent on other things.
A 0.5% levy capped at $500,000 per company per year raises a limited amount of money, likely far less than what Senate campaigns spend, so the fund might not be adequate on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — Senate campaigns funded by small donations and public money instead of by big donors and contractors — is large, and the cost is modest: a small levy on companies already profiting from federal contracts, capped so no firm pays more than $500,000 a year. The bill's main weakness is design rather than cost: the revenue earmarking is only a "sense of the Senate," not binding, so a future Congress could collect the tax without actually funding public financing. But it never advanced far enough for those details to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 6, 2011 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
A Senate Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing on April 12, 2011, but no markup or vote ever occurred in the Finance Committee.
No further action was taken before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill never received a vote in the Senate or House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large federal contractors who would have paid the excise tax, and the existing campaign-finance status quo, are better off because the bill died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large federal contractors and big donors

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 original cosponsors.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights and Human Rights
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on April 12, 2011.

for.name: 12 cosponsors (11 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Cosponsors including Boxer, Cardin, Franken, Harkin, Kerry, Klobuchar, Leahy, Merkley, Mikulski, Sanders, Shaheen, Tester

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, never holding a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-led Finance Committee never took it up.

industries.note: Companies with more than $10 million in federal contracts would pay a 0.5% excise tax on contract payments, capped at $500,000 a year [S2][S3]. Defense and other major contractors would bear most of the cost.

industries.industry: Political fundraising industry and large donors
industries.note: A publicly funded Senate campaign channel would reduce candidates' reliance on large private contributions and the consultants and fundraisers who profit from them. The bill never advanced, so this industry was unaffected.
